codex.worst_flaw: The design leaves denominator entry undefined when work starts without a checklist, so skipped checks could disappear from the rate used to award meals and decide whether to continue the rollout.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew-level meal reward can create peer pressure on individuals in small crews, and the design does not check for that pressure or for small-group inference. Its audit trail also does not keep replayable event and policy versions, and the weekly 10-visit spot check is too thin to reliably catch pencil-whipped checklists across 300 technicians.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, no-penalty stop-work credit, verified counting, private feedback, pause triggers and a staggered randomised design make it approvable, but a meal reward is modest and lasting change depends on the app workflow fixes sticking once prizes end.

codex.worst_flaw: The early reward group gets the checklist prompt and prefilled fields during the comparison window, so the trial cannot isolate the reward’s effect from those workflow improvements.

claude.worst_flaw: Each crew's weekly percentage is posted in briefing channels and the reward is an all-or-nothing 80% crew threshold, so peers can pressure each other and hazard reports may go unrecorded in small crews. The only checks on this are a 10-checklist weekly sample and an informal pressure-report trigger, and no one has to confirm that leave, excused or zero-job weeks are handled fairly.

holistic.reason: Unusually careful design with union involvement, fair counting, privacy, a randomized rollout, and a safety pause, but the one-hour reward and heavy pre-work make motivation and durability after rewards end uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: Crew-level randomisation in a 300-person company has no stated sample size, power or uncertainty handling, and the comparison window is only two weeks. Count corrections also have no replayable event or policy versions, no independent shadow validation and no staffed formal appeal, so the learning and audit claims are weakly supported.

codex.worst_flaw: Block launch because jobs completed safely using the approved paper fallback during outages still count against the crew reward, creating pressure to avoid the fallback.

holistic.reason: It is carefully designed for a unionised workforce, with stop-work credit, privacy, a fallback and a randomised rollout, but the meal reward is modest and the 80% team threshold may feel remote at 35% baseline, so awareness and motivation depend heavily on the workflow fixes and launch communication.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no way to check the clock and counts against independent data, and no staffed appeal process. On top of that, a five-review weekly quality sample with a 2-of-5 pause rule is too noisy to tell rushed reviews from normal variation. It also never measures whether faster first responses cut overall cycle time or simply move the delay to later rounds of review.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot never defines how much improvement over plain feedback would justify the paid time off, so its decision rules cannot establish whether the reward earned its cost.

holistic.reason: The proposal fixes the real workflow blockers first, keeps measurement fair, private and quality-checked, and uses a modest group reward that suits sceptical engineers, but a two-hour early finish and a Slack percentage are quiet signals, and the lasting effect depends on whether the rotation and review block actually stick.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is unfit for launch because its core metric credits approvals without an auditable standard for determining whether they reflect substantive review.

claude.worst_flaw: The audit is too small and lightly specified to catch rushed approvals or work shifting to other kinds of review: a sample of five reviews a week with a two-failure trigger checks only that the review is substantive, not defect escape or review depth on large PRs, and pausing rewards is the only recovery step.

holistic.reason: Well-designed and low-stigma (team-level time-off reward, no individual rankings, quality sampling, honest measurement plan), but it's complex to administer, relies on engineers trusting the metric, and the 'lasting' effect depends on whether routing and protected time fixes persist after rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: The evaluation leans on before-and-after comparisons within each group. Shared reviewers spill across groups, and PR volumes are small. No sample-size check, costs or harms are set in advance, so the design cannot isolate what the reward adds beyond the workflow fixes.

codex.worst_flaw: Comparing each group with its own pre-launch baseline could misattribute gains from protected review time, better routing, or private feedback to the reward.

holistic.reason: Workflow fixes first, private feedback, a transparent rule, a staggered rollout with a baseline, and an explicit quality gate suit sceptical engineers, though the small sample and the modest 90-minute reward limit how much lift and lasting effect it can show.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot is unsafe to launch because a ward can earn the reward even if its audited hand-hygiene compliance falls five percentage points below baseline, and routine audits can take a month to detect a larger drop.

claude.worst_flaw: The core adoption measure relies on auditors spotting matching kiosk entries during observation sessions. That data is collected only while observers are present, which invites Hawthorne-inflated logging, and the design names this risk but gives no independent check outside observation.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded, privacy-conscious design with workflow fixes first, ward-level reward and clear pause rules, but the one-off meal is a weak, low-salience motivator and auditor-verified sampling is operationally heavy, so habit persistence after rewards end is uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The design leaves the matching procedure and acceptable error rate undefined, so the reward should launch only after observers demonstrate that they can reliably match audited hand-hygiene events to kiosk entries without identifying staff.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk-entry-to-observed-opportunity match is the core measurement, yet there is no event history, versioned policy, shadow validation of the matching, or staffed appeal route, and the timing and matching rules for 'one corresponding entry' are left to observer judgment.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with safety gates, ward-level rewards, workflow fixes first and a post-reward check, but it is complex, the meal is a weak motivator, and the 80% verified-logging bar depends on observers being able to match kiosk entries, which may be hard to do in practice.

claude.worst_flaw: The design ties the reward to monthly observer audits but never addresses Hawthorne effects or observer bias, and never checks independently whether kiosk logging matches real hand-hygiene events. It also sets the pause and resume trigger without saying who owns the audit or how a ward's own observers are kept from inflating its score.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a valid measure of kiosk adoption because counting shifts with any entry cannot show what proportion of eligible hand-hygiene moments nurses logged.

holistic.reason: The design rewards audited compliance rather than kiosk entries, is fair to night and weekend staff, and has clear stop rules, but a single team meal is a weak, delayed motivator and the three-ward pilot cannot show much beyond a direction.

codex.worst_flaw: The uniform 40% reward threshold uses all resolved tickets without checking which tickets can usefully and safely receive an article, so case mix can determine both who earns the reward and whether the pilot appears to work.

claude.worst_flaw: The denominator counts every resolved ticket, including legitimate exceptions, so the reward pushes agents to attach articles to tickets where none fits, while the existing CSAT bonus and the knowledge-link goal are never reconciled and the only audit is a 10-ticket sample.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, a measurable team-level reward, anti-gaming QA, and a clear taper plan, though a one-hour paid-time-off reward is modest and the multi-part measurement rules are complex enough to dampen awareness and motivation.

codex.worst_flaw: The fixed 60% threshold for paid time off ignores differences in case mix and article availability, so equally diligent teams can face materially different odds of earning the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leaves the CSAT bonus unchanged and its only quality check is 12 credited tickets sampled per week, so agents can still attach articles without checking fit; nobody reviews uncredited tickets for a missing article that should have been linked, and there is no ticket-level way to catch CSAT or handle-time harm.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, quality sampling, privacy-safe feedback, and a staggered rollout with decision rules, but a two-hour team reward at a 60% threshold from a 12% baseline may feel distant and weak, and durability beyond the reward hinges on whether the workflow fixes actually make linking easy.

codex.worst_flaw: The fixed 60% reward threshold counts tickets with no safe article in the denominator, so teams can differ in their chance of earning paid time off purely because of case mix.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leaves the CSAT bonus unchanged and checks CSAT and reopens only at team level with no trigger, so agents can still send an article in place of a real answer, and a weekly sample of eight tickets across every active team is too small to catch that gaming in any one team.

holistic.reason: Well-specified counting rules, privacy-protective manager visibility, workflow fixes, staggered evaluation and QA guardrails are strong, but a one-hour paid-time-off reward for a team jump from 12% to 60% is small and the team-level collective target invites free-riding and may lose motivation, and the process is complex for 60 agents.
